The conventional parcel delivery process by trucks can be tedious due to traffic jams and lack of parking spaces, which is often the case in densely populated urban regions.
The rising volume of parcels today is primarily the result of increasing e-commerce activities.
Most online retailers offer next-day or even same-day delivery as one of their basic services.
Thus, the entire delivery process including hub-to-hub and last-mile delivery is under severe time pressure and therefore requires optimization.
Using autonomous aerial vehicles for parcel deliveries has high potential in terms of time savings, energy and cost reduction (Chiang et al., 2019, Goodchild and Toy, 2018, Müller et al., 2019).
Technological progress and the increasing number of packages to be delivered are just some of the reasons why this topic has been the focus of several investigations in recent years.
In the past five years, from 2018 until 2022, 154 engineering-oriented papers were published by Elsevier regarding drone-based delivery and autonomous drones in air logistics as visualized in Fig. 1.

A large proportion of these papers focuses on the routing problem (Attenni et al., 2023, Meng et al., 2023a, Wang and Sheu, 2019) or employs approaches on logistic optimization and scheduling (Wang et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2022).
Whereas the aforementioned topics only cover limited aspects of the technological challenges that have to be addressed, our objective is to examine a rather holistic approach in this paper.

Particularly, when it comes to multiple autonomously operating drones in a shared airspace, issues such as communication and coordination, takeoff and landing processes as well as picking up and dropping off packages have to be considered.
Based on a qualitative analysis, two important use cases for drone-based delivery were identified: long-distance hub-to-hub delivery and last-mile delivery using a truck and multi-drone tandem.
The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, the most prominent existing concepts specific to drone logistics are reviewed.
Section 3 identifies potential use cases.
Section 4 presents the specifications of use cases and quantitatively analyzes their potential.
Section 5 provides an overview of the requirements and research challenges, focusing on the previously defined use cases.
Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.
In this section, we solely focus on existing concepts specific to drone logistics, which have been addressed in the literature so far.
A detailed literature review based on the identified technical requirements and challenges within our work will follow in Section 5.
The current market situation in the logistics industry is in the process of being revolutionized by the introduction of delivery drones.
The autonomous aerial vehicles make it possible to transport packages efficiently, fast, and environment-friendly.
A leading player in this field is the company Amazon, which has been actively experimenting with drone parcel delivery for several years.
In addition, DHL and FedEx are prominent players in the drone-based parcel delivery industry as well.
Iceland’s leading eCommerce company, AHA, has teamed up with Flytrex to introduce drone deliveries in Reykjavik (Smith, 2017).
By integrating Flytrex’s drone system with their existing vehicle network, AHA has notably reduced delivery times.
In 2019, Wing, an Alphabet-owned drone company, launched Canberra’s first public drone delivery service, serving around 100 households initially (Chung et al., 2020).
UPS and Google also operate licensed drone delivery programs.
Among many start-ups actively penetrating the drone delivery market, Wingcopter has successfully partnered with various companies and secured significant investments to accelerate drone delivery.
Furthermore, the largest retail company in the US, Walmart, has been offering drone delivery services for more than two years, collaborating with multiple drone companies, including DroneUP and Wing.
Two other significant enterprises, namely Manna and Zipline, have carved out distinctive niches in the domain of drone-enabled delivery.

Manna’s specialization lies in the transportation of food and time-sensitive commodities within urban landscapes, while Zipline’s expertise shines in the domain of medical deliveries to remote and often hard-to-access regions, notably in African countries where road transportation imposes challenges.
For future large-scale drone-based package delivery applications, various concepts have been investigated.
Some of these concepts, which are mainly suitable for last-mile delivery, have been presented and thoroughly categorized by Moshref-Javadi and Winkenbach (2021).
The authors defined four distinct drone-based logistics models that shape the delivery landscape.
First, the “Pure Drone Model” entails drones delivering packages directly from a central depot to customers and then returning to the depot.
Second, the “Unsynchronized Multimodal Model” involves truck-drone tandems, operating independently.
Trucks, for instance, serve remote areas beyond the drones’ flight range.
Third, the “Synchronized Multimodal Model” uses truck-drone tandems, working collaboratively.
Lastly, the “Multimodal Resupply Model” employs an accompanying truck transporting new orders from the depot to a designated meeting point to resupply the delivery drones.

In the literature, there have been numerous studies addressing multi-drone-delivery, including drone-truck tandems, routing problems in recent years (Gao et al., 2023, Cho et al., 2022, Gonzalez-R et al., 2020, Karak and Abdelghany, 2019, Peng et al., 2019, Wen and Wu, 2022, Zang et al., 2022).
The study of Salama and Srinivas (2022) focused on truck-drone collaboration, enabling flexible truck halts for drone launch and recovery operations (LARO).
It also addresses customer location assignment, route planning for trucks and UAVs, and scheduling activities for drone LARO and truck operator tasks at each stop.
In many cases, a point-to-point operated drone can satisfy the parcel delivery requirements of customers.
However, for long distances in sparsely populated areas, a drone might require multiple recharging cycles.

The study of Alkouz et al. (2021) investigated a service-based drone delivery framework that consists of four key elements: drones as the technology behind the service, the operational environment, various types of delivery missions, and a service-oriented architecture comprising a sensor-cloud infrastructure to facilitate operations.
The authors Lee et al. (2022) introduced a framework to address drone delivery challenges, specifically aimed at generating collision-free routes within densely crowded airspace.
The approach includes gathering energy consumption data from real drone flights to establish an energy model considering drone speed and parcel weight.
A unique routing algorithm was proposed to create paths for multiple drones, accounting for individual battery capacities and route congestion.
The regulations and technologies to plan and control drone flights greatly improve the safety and security of the airspace.
In addition to Air Traffic Management (ATM) systems, the Unmanned Traffic Management (UTM) serves as a framework for managing UAV operations in uncontrolled environments.

Unlike traditional ATM in aviation, which depends on manual methods like voice communication, individual controllers, and take-off/landing permissions, the UTM introduces an ecosystem to control UAVs.
With the aim of unifying drone regulations, the European Union (EU) has formulated a shared regulatory framework.
U-Space, the European UTM concept, has already seen legislation announced in Germany for 2023.

The U-Space infrastructure includes various systems and technologies that provide a comprehensive operational and regulatory framework such as surveillance, communication, geofencing as well as identity management systems (eudroneport, 2021).
If the number of package deliveries meets our predictions, we expect a sharp rise in drone traffic in the U-Space.
This will require improved management methods to safely and effectively handle the large number of drones operating in a joint airspace.
Securing the Internet of Drones (IoD) is challenging because of changing communication standards and diverse applications.
Drones face various attack vulnerabilities.
Yang et al. (2022) discuss the potential security issues in detail and propose solutions focusing specifically on authentication and blockchain-based techniques.
The literature presents various concepts for shared airspace for secure multi-drone operations (Bauranov and Rakas, 2021).
One suggested idea is altering the usable space’s capacity over specific time frames, such as weekdays, weekends, or holidays (Vascik, 2017).

Given the numerous challenges within the parcel logistics chain, and considering that existing concepts often focus on a single aspect, such as last-mile delivery, there is a need for concepts with holistic approaches.
In the next section, we briefly highlight two specific use cases that can strongly enhance the efficiency of the standard parcel delivery process.
Standard parcel delivery services transport packages within a predetermined time window, typically larger than that of express delivery services, and this timing is not guaranteed.
In the case of express services, delivery times are guaranteed.
Another special service is the so-called ’Same-Day Delivery’, available in urban areas, where customers can pay extra for guaranteed same-day delivery.
However, offering this service conventionally everywhere is typically not profitable from both logistical and economic perspectives.
In the typical logistics process, parcels are usually brought to post centers by senders or delivery personnel.
In the collection phase, they are then transported to a specific sorting center which is considered to be the starting point for the delivery chain.
The parcels are then transported over potentially long distances to the so-called logistics hubs (delivery depots), possibly via another sorting center.
Next, the parcels are delivered from the hub to the local distribution center.
Finally, the delivery process is completed with the transportation of the parcel from the local distribution center to the recipient.

Parcel service providers in Germany and also in most European countries often use light commercial vehicles with a permissible total weight of 3.5 tons for the last-mile, which is considered to be the most energy consuming part of the overall delivery process.

The current parcel delivery process comprises several phases: long-distance (hub-to-hub) and short-distance, commonly referred to as the last-mile, transportation, and express delivery, which typically involves a combination of the first two.
In addition to these, point-to-point delivery represents a critical aspect of the logistics chain, covering transfers between distribution centers and other locations.

While last-mile delivery constitutes the most resource-demanding phase in parcel delivery, there is still significant potential for optimization in both long-distance and short-distance transportation.
Thus, we define two primary use cases: hub-to-hub and last-mile delivery.
During long-distance transportation to logistics hubs, there can be traffic-based delays that affect the delivery schedule of urgent deliveries.
Also, inefficient routing between multiple hubs can cause relatively long off-times, which can be critical for express deliveries.
Drone delivery for long-distance transport between logistics hubs may offer a compelling solution ensuring timely delivery of urgent parcels.
For this purpose, fixed-wing vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) drones with the appropriate payload can be deployed and operated on-demand as a part of the logistics process.

The distinct advantages of integrating long-distance delivery with fixed-wing VTOL drones are coverage of hard-to-reach areas for crucial or time-sensitive goods, lower infrastructure dependency (no need for runway), flexibility, and reduced environmental impact for urgent transportation situations.
Furthermore, UAV autonomy streamlines delivery operations, reduces personnel costs, optimizes routes (especially in last-mile delivery), and fulfills evolving logistics industry needs.
This leads to improved efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and customer satisfaction in the changing landscape of delivery services.
The analyses on drone delivery based on Amazon Prime Air have already indicated that it can reduce costs by one-third or more compared to ground delivery (Sudbury and Hutchinson, 2016).
A recent study in China forecasts a reduction in total cost and delivery time by 22.13% and 20.65%, respectively, compared to truck delivery (Meng et al., 2023b).
Additionally, the study by Chiang et al. (2019) shows that UAV delivery systems can significantly reduce energy consumption and lower CO2 emissions.

The demand for flexible and innovative concepts in drone delivery arises from the need to adapt to diverse use-cases, especially in challenging urban environments and the last-mile phase (Chi et al., 2023).
These concepts prioritize sustainability, safety, and regulatory compliance while enhancing the customer experience and aligning with needs of the logistics industry.
While drone delivery is a promising logistics concept for enhancing efficiency especially in the last-mile, it faces limitations when employed solely without the support of other means.
According to a survey, many people do not have the ability to provide a special area for the landing maneuvers of drones (Seidakhmetov and Valilai, 2022).
In addition, drones have restrictions in terms of payload capacity, flight range, and uncertain weather conditions.
To overcome these limitations, drones can be integrated into the conventional delivery system with humans using auxiliary vehicles such as trucks or mobile robots.
Trucks provide a larger payload capacity and extend the range of service.
Moreover, they can function as mobile micro-hubs and stations for charging and maintenance.
This collaborative approach can combine multiple technologies optimizing the standalone drone delivery.
In the article of Joerss et al. (2016), delivery models based on ground vehicles, drones, and couriers were determined to be suitable in future applications.
Use Case 1: Hub(X)-to-X-Transport by long-range suitable drones.
To tackle the challenges outlined in the previous chapter, two drone-based use cases are presented, which address long-range transportation as well as last-mile delivery.
In this section, we define these use cases, some of which are already known in this or a similar form in recent literature.
Subsequently, the question of how these use cases meet the requirements in the field of parcel logistics in the upcoming future is addressed.

Afterwards, a data-based demand analysis is conducted to substantiate the proposed approaches and to give an indication of the future volume of drone traffic, especially near central handling points (hubs).
The “Hub(X)-to-X-Transport” concept focuses on courier services and the transport of goods employing long-range suitable drones.
This use case considers four scenarios, which all have the same technical requirements for the drone.
Therefore, all scenarios can be served utilizing the same type of long-range drone.
The scenarios mainly differ in the distance between the start and the goal location.
The variants of the use case are illustrated in Fig. 2.
**E-Commerce Delivery**: Direct point-to-point delivery from a local warehouse to the customer.
This scenario is already applied by companies such as Amazon and Zipline.
**Medium Range Express-Service**: Transport of goods from an arbitrary point of origin to a central logistics hub, from where the final delivery to the customer takes place.
**Courier Delivery**: Direct point-to-point delivery from an arbitrary point of origin to the customer.
This scenario corresponds to a standard courier delivery.
As soon as requested, a drone will take off at the service provider and pick up the parcel at the point of origin.
From there, it will conduct the delivery to the customer.
**Long-Range Express-Service**: Transport of goods from an arbitrary point of origin or another logistics hub to the destination hub by truck.
This scenario takes into account all deliveries that would exceed the operating range of the commonly used drones.
When the parcel reaches the destination hub by truck, a drone will conduct the final delivery process to the customer.
All scenarios listed above and their possible deployment are highly dependent on the potential range requirements.
In the paper of Schuh et al. (2022), a range of 100 km was considered.

For this research, a potential range of 135 km is assumed, which allows one-way deliveries of 120 km (including charging at the destination hub) and deliveries within a radius of 60 km using a round trip.
The assumption includes a safety buffer for unfavorable wind conditions and the increased energy demand for take-off and landing according to Kirschstein (2021).
Due to their aerodynamic design and the resulting energy efficiency for long-distance flights, fixed-wing VTOL drones are proposed for this application.
It is also possible to deploy a set of different fixed-wing drones that have varying capacities depending on the required weight and distance to be covered.
By assigning the most suitable drone to each scenario, energy efficiency can be optimized.
In contrast to ground-based delivery, drone-based deliveries can be conducted independently of other packages and are not subject to delays that could be caused by road traffic.
This offers significant time savings compared to conventional delivery methods.

A possible application field where no time delays can be tolerated is medical applications, such as the transport of medications (Gatteschi et al., 2015), medical device (Fischer et al., 2023), or even blood (Ling and Draghic, 2019).
In the production industry, the transport of tools or spare parts can be highly time-critical, for example, in case of a machine failure (Freichel et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the use of long-distance drones can be particularly advantageous in regions with poor road conditions or in the event of a natural disaster that affects the road network (Rabta et al., 2018).
By deploying multiple autonomously operating drones in a hybrid model, it is possible to deliver packages in a shorter time compared to conventional delivery.
In this way, the steadily increasing number of packages to be delivered can be better met.

By optimizing the main route and eliminating the need for the truck to individually visit each destination point, the overall distance traveled is minimized, resulting in energy and emission savings for the truck.
To exploit the potential of drone-based delivery while addressing its limitations, use case 2 “Decentralized delivery via truck-drone tandem” is presented.
It consists of two scenarios that are depicted in Fig. 3.
Both of them focus on parcel delivery in the last-mile.

This truck-drone tandem concept has already been the focus of several investigations (Campbell et al., 2018, Moshref-Javadi et al., 2021, Murray and Raj, 2020), especially in the context of route planning, as mentioned in Section 2.
The approach of this paper, however, addresses the process holistically in order to identify research gaps and necessary interfaces.
The infrastructure of the first scenario is composed of the main route and some static or dynamic distribution points.
The transport truck features a load compartment for parcels and space for landing, loading and transporting drones.
The truck drives along the route and stops at every distribution point.
From there, drones start delivering packages in the surrounding area of the distribution point and return to the truck afterwards to automatically pick up further packages.
The transport vehicle acts as a mobile micro-hub.
If the truck continues to move along the main route to increase efficiency while the drones are delivering packages, this is considered a dynamic distribution point.
The second scenario differs in the sense that both the drones and the transport vehicle are actively delivering packages.
The main route is planned such that the packages that are not suitable for delivery by drone are delivered in the conventional way by the driver of the transport vehicle.
This way, the second use case takes into account packages exceeding the loading weight or the maximum possible dimensions for drone-based delivery.
Customers who do not have the spatial requirements for receiving drone-delivered packages are considered too.
Whenever drone-based delivery is not possible or desired, packages can be processed in the conventional way by the truck-driver.
Dynamic or static distribution points are also possible in this scenario.

Since autonomously operating drones are not dependent on road infrastructure, they have the potential to conduct the delivery process of parcels more cost- and time-efficiently than the conventional ground-based approach with a truck.
State-of-the-art drones still have relatively limited flight times.
Using them in a collaborative fashion in a fleet of ground-based vehicles tackles this problem.
In this way, drones can overcome their limitations in terms of payload capacity, flight range and battery capacity by working in tandem with a truck.
The truck functions as a mobile depot and provides recharging possibility.
This is advantageous since the truck is also able to deliver goods that are not suitable for air transport due to their size, weight, or chemical characteristics (flammable).
For this use case, where relatively short distances are covered, multicopter drones are preferable to fixed-wing drones.
This section provides quantitative support for the need and the necessity of the two use cases.
The results of the investigations serve as reference values to determine the number of parcels that would be handled by the drone-based use cases.
Based on this, required technologies will be derived and research gaps will be identified.
For this purpose, data from the logistics sector and from published studies are analyzed.

To determine the primary demand conditions of Use Case 1, which focuses on drone-based long-distance delivery between hubs and various destinations, available data from the courier, express, and parcel (CEP) sector was processed and analyzed.
Since the information about CEP deliveries are strongly dependent of region and population, this investigation was limited to Germany.
The information provided by the German Parcel and Express Logistics Association (Bundesverband Paket und Expresslogistik e.V. (BIEK)) was used as reference.

Since this analysis only serves as a reference point for further considerations regarding the necessary technologies for a drone-based delivery process, the results can be transferred to countries with similar framework conditions.
In Germany, around 4.5 billion CEP shipments were transported in 2022.
In terms of weight and volume, these are small, sometimes time-critical deliveries with weights of up to 31.5 kg.
They include letters, small packages, and parcels.
Heavier freight is assigned to a different logistics category.
According to BIEK, the average weight of a CEP shipment in 2022 was around 5 kg.
The proportion of heavy parcels, weighing over 20 kg, constitutes 5% of the total CEP shipments.
Deutsche Post DHL operates 38 parcel centers in Germany (DHL Group, 2022), in close proximity to which the hubs of other parcel service providers can also be found for strategic reasons.
In order to derive statements regarding the utilization of a possible drone logistics hub based on the BIEK data, some assumptions were made (Table 1).
The investigations focus on the DHL hubs.
Since the information about exact proportion of deliveries transported between cities or hubs, is not publicly available, it is assumed that this accounts for 95% of all CEP shipments.
In addition, it is assumed that the shipments are distributed according to the population shares of the federal states and that each hub supplies the federated state in which it is located.
Moreover, it is assumed that a drone transport covers at maximum the distance between two neighboring hubs.
Longer distances are covered by other means of transport such as trucks, as mentioned in the definition of the first use case.

According to data provided by BIEK, the proportion of courier and express deliveries, which in contrast to ordinary parcel deliveries are eligible for the long-distance drone transport, is 14.7% of total CEP deliveries.
Considering the aforementioned assumptions, the estimated annual count of CEP deliveries viable for drone-based long-distance transportation in Germany is approximately 90.5 million.
This leads to the estimated values for daily and hourly hub utilization (refer to Table 2).
The calculation considers the quantity of CEP deliveries per federal state (factoring in population density and the number of hubs in each state).
In addition, it is assumed that daily flight operation of 12 hours with up to three parcels bundled per flight is feasible.
According to Schuh et al. (2022), a maximum flight speed of 130 km/h was assumed for the calculations as well as an average flight distance of 60 km, including the way back to the hub.
Assuming evenly distributed distances between the starting point and the delivery location, the number of required long-distance drones can be approximated, as shown in Table 2.
The figures demonstrate the potential of this use case.
According to the calculations, an estimated average demand of approximately 200 drone flights per hour is expected for a DHL delivery hub.
To meet this demand, a DHL hub would need to have an average of 91 long-distance drones available.
In regions where the ratio of inhabitants per hub is large, up to a potential maximum of 660 flights per hour can be expected.

To outline the second use case, numerous sources were analyzed and a supporting data preparation was performed.
Referring to the study of Doole et al. (2018) on airspace density, certain assumptions and data are used to provide quantitative support for last-mile delivery considerations.
In 2021, the share of parcels dispatched in urban areas that weighed 2.2 kg or less was approximately 3.1 billion.
The specified weight limit is taken from ongoing projects exploring deliveries within urban areas.
In the study of Narkus-Kramer (2017), it was hypothesized that 70% of urban parcel deliveries could potentially be facilitated through drone delivery.
The essential data for estimating quantitative values concerning daily parcel delivery, the number of parcels per person, and parcel volume per area for different German cities are shown in Table 3.
This selection encompasses a big city, a mid-size city, and a small town, chosen as comparative references.
Using the provided data and sources, logistics indicators are derived.
These key figures constitute the potential number of packages that could be transported through decentralized delivery in the hybrid last-mile model.
The scalability of this use case across various population densities is attainable through the modification of the number of vehicles, making it fundamentally applicable to cities of all sizes.
To elaborate on the numbers of truck-drones-tandems to satisfy the operational demand, the previously obtained data is applied in further calculations.
To generate an estimation of these numbers for each of the three aforementioned urban areas, we applied the following assumptions.
The daily operating period is assumed to be 12 h per day.
Another premise is made for the configuration of the truck-drone-tandems.
Each of them consists of one truck and two multi-copter drones.
This assumption is derived based on technical requirements related to the drones and trucks.
For simplicity, a uniform distribution of the parcel destinations within the urban areas is assumed, taking into account the average population density and the number of parcels per day.
In a simulation for each of the three reference cities distribution points for the truck-drone tandems are determined using an optimization algorithm.
Based on this, the average flight distances of the drones are calculated.
According to the research of Tamke and Buscher (2023), an average flight speed of 12 m/s (43,2 km/h) can be assumed for the drones in this scenario.

Also, in addition to the pure flight time, the service time 90 s for a drone delivery is taken into account, which covers the duration of landing, dropping the parcel and relaunching at a customer location.
The time for the preparation of a drone at the truck is also assumed to be 90 s.
Based on these assumptions, it is possible to determine the average delivery capacity per drone in one hour for each of the reference cities.
In Ingolstadt for example, one drone of the tandem is able to deliver approximately 17 parcels per hour.
According to DHL employees a driver of a truck delivers in average 24 parcels per hour in the conventional way.
In addition to the parcels delivered by the drones, the tandem is able to handle a total of approximately 58 parcels per hour.
These calculations only relate to the average number of parcels that can be delivered per hour.
As the drones themselves and the corresponding equipment, such as exchange batteries, also occupy space in the truck, this reduces the total number of parcels that can be transported.
This must be taken into account when designing the trucks of truck-drone-tandems.

Otherwise, if the size of the truck remains the same as a conventional delivery truck, it would have to be taken into account that the reduced loading volume could make reloading trips to the parcel center necessary.
Assuming a delivery capacity of approximately 58 parcels per hour the utilization of a truck-drone-tandem increases the performance to 240%, compared to a conventional delivery truck.
Based on the number of parcels to be delivered per hour and the average capacity of a tandem, the number of required tandems for each city can be determined.
