The results serve as a reference to determine the size of the required fleet in order to meet the average daily package volume.
However, additional aspects, which would increase the number of tandems to be procured, need to be considered for realization.
These include for example the breakdown of technical components or regular maintenance as well as increased package volume (e.g., during Christmas season).
In addition, the time required for reloading the truck with parcels and charging or exchanging drone batteries must be taken into account for a detailed process design.
Both identified use cases increase the complexity of logistics planning.
To make the drone-based transportation more viable, a number of prerequisites must be satisfied.
Some of these do not play a role in the process of conventional delivery methods.
In addition, the parameters that determine the suitability of drone-based delivery can already be taken into account in the early planning process, which might increase the complexity even more.
These parameters include, for example, the weight and dimensions of a parcel, which may not exceed certain values depending on the drone.
The suitability and distance of the destination for delivery by drone is also crucial.
Deliveries in rural regions are easier to manage than deliveries in urban regions.
Regulatory restrictions such as certain no-fly zones can prevent air transportation.
These and further similar aspects need to be integrated into the existing planning process and logistics networks.

In this regard, there is already a number of studies in the literature that address the routing problem (Attenni et al., 2023, Meng et al., 2023a, Wang and Sheu, 2019) or employ approaches on logistic optimization and scheduling (Wang et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2022).
In the long term, it can also be assumed that the increasing usage of drones or truck-drone tandems will reduce the need for conventional delivery trucks, especially in the last-mile.
However, they would still serve their purpose in carrying out transports for which drone-based delivery is not an option, such as long distances or particularly large and heavy goods.
Nevertheless, it should be noted that the number of parcels to be delivered will continue to rise in the future, as the historic data and projection from Statista (2024) indicates.
The demand for advanced delivery methods, such as the two use cases analyzed, has already been examined in the previous subsections.
In addition, the economic feasibility of such a technology plays a decisive role in its success, as does the relationship between savings and costs compared to conventional delivery methods.
The studies of Dong et al. (2021) deal with the impact of emerging and disruptive technologies on transportation and emphasize the promising cost and time savings that drone-based transport offers.
By implementing the analyzed use cases into logistics, considerable savings can be expected, such as lower labor costs for personnel and lower operating costs for vehicles.
For the truck drone approach, our analyses have already shown that such a tandem increases the performance of a conventional truck up to 240%.
The parcels delivered by the drones in this scenario reduce the workload on the drivers and at the same time the number of drivers required, which reduces personnel costs.
Apart from the one-time acquisition costs for the drones, certain operating costs are to be expected.
These can cover maintenance, infrastructure, and labor costs (drone specialists).
To get an accurate idea of potential costs and savings, a dedicated analysis of each use case discussed here is required.
Currently, the literature barely addresses these.
An analysis of the maintenance costs for drone delivery from 2019 indicates a cost of 0.06 $/km while the maintenance costs for a truck is approximately 0.12 $/km (Butcher and Lim, 2019).
There are potentially unexplored cost savings on drone deliveries cutting back on overtime that remain unexplored.
Moreover, fuel and driver costs can create savings that can be investigated thoroughly.
However, it is important to note that a study by Figliozzi et al. (2018) indicates the benefits of economies of scale may be countered by increased safety risks.
Additionally, concerns related to privacy, safety, and noise are more pronounced in urban areas, though they may not be as significant in rural settings.
Based on the use case analysis conducted in Section 4 and the expected air traffic volumes, we discuss the technical requirements and identify potential research gaps within this section.
Particular attention is paid to the autonomy of the drones, which we consider to be necessary for drone delivery becoming a viable business model.
These autonomous drone systems must meet high safety requirements and minimize air and ground risks even in the event of a failure of critical functions.

Since the airspace has to be shared with other, and in the future increasingly autonomous, air traffic participants, also suitable coordination measures are required that take the U-Space concept into account.

Before we address requirements in the relevant technical areas and highlight potential research gaps in Section 5.2, we first address the requirements for ground and air risk reduction as well as the U-Space concept in the following section.
An overview of the key requirements and technological considerations is depicted in Fig. 4.
In air logistics with UAVs, operations in U-Space are essential for safely coordinating flights.
Given that a majority of operations occur in urban airspaces, careful consideration of air and ground risks is of great importance within the overall framework.

Since logistics drones are intensively operated in urban airspace, the potential risks with regard to other airspace users, the environment, properties, but also with regard to people on the ground are of interest.
In this context, the division of urban airspace into altitude ranges of 120 to 300 m has undergone examination by Schuh et al. (2022).

This investigation focuses on a geometry-based description of operational space, potentially influencing flight route design and procedures, as well as impacting the permissible volume of aircraft operations within the airspace .

In another study (Kobaszyńska-Twardowska et al., 2022), a pioneering multi-criteria risk model is introduced, providing a foundational framework for further developments in risk management methodology.

Geister and Korn (2017) present another concept that divides the airspace into mobile sub-areas based on drone-specific factors such as the technological capabilities and represents each drone with safety ellipsoid.
The literature has extensively explored also ground risk assessments (Han et al., 2022), delving into a risk-based analysis of potential UAV flight corridors over densely populated regions.
The analysis of Kim and Bae (2022) considers factors such as population density, flight restrictions, and emergency response capabilities.
Another investigation (Li et al., 2023) undertook a comprehensive ground risk assessment for UAVs, incorporating various risk sources.
The research aimed to evaluate and analyze conceivable risks linked to UAV operations across diverse environments.
Employing a systematic methodology, this approach assessed ground risks by taking into account factors such as terrain conditions, proximity to infrastructure, and potential hazards.

In automated drone logistics for both long-distance express delivery (use case 1) and last-mile delivery (use case 2), Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) capabilities play an essential role for emergency cases.
In BVLOS operations, the capability to operate UAVs beyond the operator’s direct line of sight, without the aid of a visual observer, opens up new frontiers.
The consideration of BVLOS underscores its foundational role in enhancing the capabilities and applications of drones in logistics, particularly in scenarios requiring immediate remote solutions.
Secure control in BVLOS scenarios depends on employing reliable communication and sensing technologies, like the Remote Pilot Station (RPS) or Ground Control Station (GCS).

A significant gap in current research exists regarding the development of air and ground risk assessment models for operation of multi-drone applications and the exploration of new technical systems specifically designed for risk mitigation.
Section 5.2.4 provides an overview of the overall technical requirements in this context.
Ensuring safe operations within the U-Space, the designated airspace for drones stands as a critical concern for UAV activities.
This becomes especially crucial when considering the challenges posed by multiple drones operated by different service providers with different technical properties and capabilities.
There have been various attempts to propose new airspace designs and concepts in the literature.
One of the considerations involves segmenting the airspace into sections and designating specific types of drones or services to each section (Krozel et al., 2008).
Metron Aviation suggested that the design of procedures and communications, navigation, and surveillance capabilities are factors that can affect airspace capacity.
The PansaUTM system has pioneered the development of a nationwide integrated ATM and UTM system (Unmanned-Airspace, 2021).
It features functions such as “OVERDUE”, providing UAV pilots with information about tower-accepted clearance times to minimize unauthorized flights.
An automatic capacity management function regulates automatic permits within controlled airport zones.

In addition, the system offers reduced flight planning time for emergency services and law enforcement, as well as a super-pilot feature to reduce planning time for frequently operating drone operators and pilots.

Within the U-Space operations, a range of UAV attributes can be taken into consideration, providing insights that have been integrated into a multi-drone simulation model, as demonstrated by Kuru et al. (2019).
These attributes include elements like the UAV’s unique identifier (ID), maximum flight duration, access to local network information, and reservation status.
The UAV’s ID serves as a distinctive marker for identification.
The maximum flight duration sets the limit on how long a UAV can operate continuously before requiring recharging.
The accessibility to local network information defines the UAV’s ability to access local data such as maps or weather updates.
The reservation status indicates whether the UAV is currently assigned to a specific customer or not.
These aspects can play an important role in the context of UTM, in the control, performance, and mission planning of UAVs in shared airspace.
With the increasing utilization of airspace by UAVs, the need for reliable **autonomous capabilities**, real-time risk assessment and mitigation strategies cannot be neglected.
U-Space aims to achieve this by using a comprehensive network of networked sensors, data exchange platforms and advanced algorithms to assess potential threats both in the air and on the ground.

To ensure the technologies are tested in conditions close to their intended use cases and to gather valuable insights from these new systems, the establishment of practical U-Spaces and the implementation of related regulations is also essential.
These measures will allow for the real-world application and continual refinement of U-Space initiatives, fostering a safer and more efficient integration of autonomous UAVs into the airspace.

Given that AI-based systems are commonly employed in most autonomy applications such as decision making, scene understanding, planning, the trustworthiness of these systems is a significant concern, especially in safety critical areas.

To avoid mostly unpredictable, dangerous consequences, EASA is actively engaged in formulating guidance for the use such systems in aviation, underlining their commitment to ensuring safety and regulatory alignment in autonomous applications (EASA, 2021).
The challenges in ensuring trustworthiness for AI-based functionalities in drones are usually due to the limitations posed by black-box deep learning models.
To address these challenges, Explainable AI (XAI) methods have emerged (Ottun et al., 2023), where such models are generated that humans can easily understand and trust (Arrieta et al., 2020).
In the aviation context, EASA introduced two key building blocks for ensuring trustworthy AI applications: AI Trustworthiness Analysis and AI Assurance Concept.
The former involves characterizing AI, safety, security, and ethics assessments, emphasizing human oversight.
The latter addresses learning assurance and development explainability, ensuring AI-based systems produce reliable results and supporting ongoing safety monitoring (EASA, 2023).

The existing aerospace certification standards and methodologies, originally designed with classical approaches, struggle to adequately adapt to the ongoing transition to non-deterministic autonomous systems.

The key difficulties in certification involve the lack of a comprehensive guideline for requirement tracing, inadequacies in current systems methodologies to handle dynamic requirements and validation of AI-enabled systems (Henderson et al., 2022).

The gap in current research centers around the development of a certification framework for AI with a confidence-driven approach, encompassing the complete, well-documented set of airworthiness criteria, and compliance methods needed to evaluate the safety and airworthiness of a specific system.
To maximize profits in drone-based logistics business models, **autonomy** and minimal personnel intervention are highly important.

To achieve these objectives, integration of advanced environment sensing technologies, path planning, decision making, precise self-localization algorithms, reliable communication protocols within shared airspace, and data exchange with other airspace users are required.
The technology fields necessary for autonomy, in accordance with the framework discussed in Section 5.1, are further addressed in the following.
For each field of technology, the requirements resulting from the use case study are first discussed, existing technical solutions are presented and research gaps are identified.
In order to gather information about the environment, sensors onboard the drone as well as additional ground-based sensors can be employed.
The sensor equipment provides the basic data for some functionalities such as path planning (Section 5.2.2), task assignment (Section 5.2.3) and localization (Section 5.2.6).
The required equipment and its capabilities can vary depending on the application and the accuracy requirements of the sensor data.
In order to provide an indication of the technically required sensor properties, we assume that a detection range of 400 m is sufficient for a long-range drone (use case 1).

This assumption is based on the maximum flight speed of 130 km/h, which leads to a time buffer of approximately 11 s to identify and react (change heading, decelerate) to an object that is detected in 400 m distance.
It should be considered that the duration of the process for identifying and reacting to an object is highly dependent on the data acquisition and data processing frequency of the drone.

The generation of a reactive control signal can take several seconds, starting with the acquisition of information from a sensor, followed by the fusion with data from other sensors, processing in a tracking algorithm and integration into path planning.
Assuming that a flying object is detected moving directly towards the drone, the time buffer is reduced to a minimum of 5.5 s, which is still considered sufficient.
Detection ranges of up to 400 m are feasible with the current state-of-the-art for range detection sensors such as lidars and radars.

For drone based last-mile delivery (use case 2) employing slower flight speeds, the detection range could be scaled down to 200 m, which will result in smaller sensors that are also less weight and power consuming.
However, it is recommended not to reduce the detection range below 200 m, even at lower speeds, especially considering the increased risk when operating in urban areas.
Onboard sensors, ranging from cameras, lidars, radars and radio receivers to thermal imaging devices, gather precise real-time data (Yasin et al., 2020).
They are necessary to enable the drone to operate independently.
Otherwise – assuming a purely ground-controlled drone – a malfunction of the communication connection could lead to a total breakdown of the drone.
Nevertheless, the use of sensor equipment on a drone is limited by primarily two aspects.
On the one hand, the weight of the sensors is a limiting factor, as there is only a limited capacity for sensors onboard a drone.

On the other hand, the sensor data is only useful and reliable if the raw data is merged using sensor data fusion (Du et al., 2020) or analyzed in other ways, such as semantic segmentation (Hao et al., 2020).
This often requires complex calculation methods that are intensive in terms of computing capacity and power consumption, which are also limiting factors onboard a drone.

Nevertheless, ground-based sensors can contribute to the efficiency and accuracy of drone operations, as demonstrated in the study of Kong et al. (2013) and Zhang et al. (2019), especially when employed in hub areas or onboard a truck (truck-drone tandem).
A particularly high level of risk arises from the operation of drones when they are flying close to the ground or in airspace with high flight density, i.e. during take-off and landing at drone hubs.
Ground-based sensors can function as an additional information source by detecting drones and other flying objects in critical areas.

With regard to the sensor equipment, future studies should address the identification and implementation of the most suitable sensor systems to enhance safety, navigation, and overall use-case-specific performance.
The development of smaller and lighter sensor systems and new innovative sensor technologies, such as so-called frequency modulated continuous wave (FMCW) lidar systems, offer further potential.
Moreover, current research lacks guidelines for the minimum required capabilities (sensor equipment) to operate a cargo drone safely in urban airspace.

Alongside with these investigations, methods for environmental perception should also be further improved in order to meet requirements of the use cases mentioned above and ensure the safe operation of drones in densely occupied areas.

Algorithms for environmental perception by drones, such as semantic segmentation, voxel maps, etc., have made great progress in recent years — partly due to the deployment of AI-based approaches, which also hold potential for further research, as mentioned in Section 5.1.3.
Path planning for logistics drones is a significant requirement in optimizing routes, ensuring deliveries in the shortest and safest possible way.
This involves utilizing available sensors and other information to facilitate the entire delivery process, including takeoff, landing, and delivery, which must operate in great harmony.
High operation precision is essential not only for the individual performance of drones but also for the routing of truck-drone tandems.
To ensure a highly harmonic behavior in dense urban airspaces, proper path planning and coordination of certain sub-processes can ease many technical and operational challenges.
As analyzed in Section 4.3, an estimated average demand of approximately 200 drone flights per hour is projected.
To manage the flights in such relatively congested airspace above the hub area, appropriate path and motion planning strategies should be developed and tested.
In UAV path planning, prioritizing Air/Ground Risk Reduction and Unmanned Traffic Management are key aspects.
Routes should consider minimizing risks and ensuring access to emergency landing sites within a specified, technically possible timeframe.
Strategies for handling of communication failures should also be integrated to the planner, emphasizing autonomous behavior and alternative methods for safe guidance in adverse scenarios.
Challenges related to path planning include limited flight time, crash risks, and the need to operate in uncertain conditions.

To address these, researcher have proposed various approaches in the literature, ranging from Model Predictive Control (MPC) (Bertrand et al., 2014) to schemes based on Control Barrier Function (CBF) (Ames et al., 2019, Dawson et al., 2023) and deep reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2019a), in the development motion planning algorithms suitable for UAVs.

For path planning, methodologies frequently employ well-established approaches like the A* algorithm (Mandloi et al., 2021) and the Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT) algorithm to navigate through complex scenarios (LaValle, 2006).
**Centralized** approaches involve the collection, analysis, and distribution of data and commands from a single, centralized point of control (Salamat and Elsbacher, 2022).
Since a truck-drone tandem like in use case 2 is a rigid team (each truck collaborates with the same drones), scalability is not a significant issue.

With centralized coordination, critical processes such as take-off, landing, and parcel loading can be managed from a holistic view of the entire system at the centralized control entity (e.g., at a truck).
Moreover, centralized control minimizes the potential for conflicts and maximizes the overall efficiency and safety of UAV operations in increasingly crowded and complex urban and rural environments.
Centralized control approaches have been usually developed to achieve high-precision coordination of UAV fleets (Ang et al., 2018, Zhao et al., 2019).
Yanmaz et al. (2017) tested a centralized approach, where the routes of all UAVs are pre-computed on the ground station and then sent to the drones’ on-board control for execution.
In case of communication interruption or configuration changes, centralized approaches are prone to failure.
**Decentralized** path planning refers to an approach where the decision-making process for determining optimal paths is distributed among individual entities within a system.
Decentralized methods can be beneficial for both use cases due to several reasons.
Firstly, long-distance drone transportation (use case 1) involves multiple drones operating over a large geographical area.
Coordinating the tasks, routes, and actions of these drones centrally can be challenging and prone to delays.
Secondly, weather conditions, or local changes in airspace regulations during the long-distance flights can be handled autonomously if decentralized coordination skills are available.
Furthermore, decentralized coordination avoids vulnerabilities and congestion that may come with a centralized approach.
By optimizing the path planning in the last-mile delivery, the goal is to improve the customer satisfaction (Garg et al., 2023).

Also in the delivery phase of the last-mile operations (use case 2), decentralized approaches can provide better scalability and robustness against failures of individual components of the operation (truck or other drones of the tandem).
By distributing coordination tasks among the UAVs, the system can handle more transportation operations while remaining robust and reliable.
This collaborative method has the potential of increasing the accuracy and resilience, emphasizing reliability through redundancy against signal disruptions or interference.

The majority of studies in the field of decentralized control concentrate on topics such as UAV formation (Muslimov and Munasypov, 2021, Wu et al., 2023a, Wu et al., 2023b) and area coverage path planning for search and inspection tasks (Olcay et al., 2020, Hu et al., 2022, Ivić et al., 2023, Qin and Pournaras, 2023).
However, in the specific context of decentralized coordination of logistics UAVs and task allocation, there is a need for more research with experimental results.

This indicates a gap in the literature and highlights the importance of further studies in this area to enhance our understanding of how logistics UAVs can be effectively coordinated and allocated tasks in a decentralized manner.
To optimize routing and planning operations in the use cases under consideration, leveraging the potential of AI can be a significant enhancement (see Section 5.1.3).

Although the centralized and decentralized methods can provide different advantages in subprocesses of the use cases under consideration, hybrid approaches, combination of centralized and decentralized together, can be adopted to have a more adaptive behavior.
Furthermore, the trade-off between functionality and the cost due to the need for relatively high computational power for the central control unit is a further direction for investigation.
In addition, dynamic uncooperative flying objects, such as birds or other drones should also be considered in planning.
Another key aspect revolves around the automation of task assignment to efficiently orchestrate the activities of drones in a shared operation and provide input for the path planner.

The primary goal of automating task assignment is to increase the efficiency of drone fleets, taking into account crucial considerations such as payload capacity, battery status, and kinematic constraints.
By breaking down the overall mission objective into individual tasks assigned to each drone, this process enables efficient resource utilization, enhances adaptability and collective performance.
Based on our estimation in Section 4.3, a drone operated in a city should accomplish a task (one parcel delivery) in approximately 3.5 min.
So the task planner should organize the tasks accordingly.

Several studies have examined how tasks should be assigned in truck-drone cooperation systems for parcel delivery (Bai et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2019b), with some also considering the impact of stochastic customer request patterns (Grippa et al., 2019).
Task allocation mechanisms usually rely on sophisticated algorithms and numerical methods.
By considering the payload capacity of individual drones, the system can allocate tasks that fall within the weight restrictions of each drone.
This prevents overburdening and increases the drones’ stability during flight.

In the study of Awada et al. (2023), drones with edge devices are used for resource-intensive tasks, and a machine learning model helps optimize their scheduling and execution, resulting in faster task completion and better resource utilization.
Furthermore, the battery status is another critical element to be considered within the mission assignment process.
Gonzalez-R et al. (2020) as well as Ma and Chen (2023) addressed both constrained power life and energy minimization aspects within the task and route assignment context.
By evaluating the remaining battery life of each drone, the mechanism can prioritize tasks and assign drones with sufficient power to fulfill them.
This guarantees continuous operation and prevents premature battery discharge.
Task assignment processes for UAVs need to take into account factors related to kinematic constraints.
Each drone owns distinct motion capabilities and physical boundaries that must be considered to prevent collisions, ensure safe trajectories, and uphold the desired performance standards.

By considering kinematic constraints, such as maximum speed, turning radius, and maneuvering capabilities, the mechanism can determine suitable paths and coordination strategies for the parcel delivery operation.

Further research is needed to extend existing task scheduling and allocation algorithms for truck-drone tandems on a larger scale so that each truck-drone tandem exchanges information with other truck-drone tandems operating in the same region, thus optimizing the entire logistics process in a holistic way.
In the case of communication or connection failures during a mission, the importance of robust safety protocols becomes clear.
This involves integrating various safety measures, including parachute deployment, to ensure effective emergency landings in case of total onboard system breakdown.
However, parachute-based systems bring about concerns over uncontrolled free fall and vulnerability to strong winds.
It has been suggested that drones should maintain continuous flight for at least 30 s to enable a safe emergency landing, potentially safer than relying solely on parachutes.

For collision avoidance, audible warning signals can also be beneficial, alongside the adoption of advanced aviation technologies like flight alarm (FLARM) for sailplanes and Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) for passenger aircrafts.

Emergency procedures for transport drones should address crucial aspects such as failure detection, adaptive flight control with disturbance observer, and condition monitoring to trigger an emergency landing.
Autonomous detection of suitable landing spots is significant feature for an efficient and safe emergency landing.
Establishing a time standard for reaching detected landing spots can strongly vary based on the emergency case (engine quit, defect rotor) and the technical properties of the drone.

Consideration of drone type (multicopter vs. fixed-wing) is essential, with specific attention to propulsion-based flight or gliding towards a landing spot, whose optimal size depends on the size of the drone.

The incorporation of autonomous emergency landing capability for UAVs represents a significant technological advancement aimed at enhancing the safety and dependability of unmanned aerial transportation as well as reducing the air and ground risks.
The introduction of automated emergency landing procedures for UAVs marks a pioneering development, with a limited number of commercial applications presently available in the market.
Only a handful of strategies for the autonomous emergency landing of drones have been documented within the scientific literature (Dhami et al., 2022, Kaljahi et al., 2019).
One such approach involves the integration of cameras and artificial intelligence (AI), as presented by Hausmann et al. (2022).
Within the method, the identification of a suitable landing site is achieved through a combination of real-time semantic environmental sensing, mapping and logical decision-making processes.

The authors Matsumoto and Premachandra (2023) proposed a method for estimating ground unevenness for emergency landing purposes, which uses depth information acquired from a depth camera and employs machine learning and statistical processing techniques.
The investigations of Alam and Oluoch (2021) provide insights into various types of landing zones and the techniques used for detecting them in UAVs.
It also reviews some of the existing zone detection algorithms for outdoor applications.

Although the system monitoring and automatic detection of anomalies are essential parts of emergency procedures, there are limited studies on condition monitoring for drones (Bondyra et al., 2017, Pourpanah et al., 2018).

The research gap lies in the application and testing of data-driven approaches employing signal processing and machine learning techniques not only for emergency case detection but also for ensuring safe package delivery.
Moreover, safe landing spot and delivery detection using vision-based methods still requires further research effort to take a step towards commercialization.
The ability to take-off and land on a mobile hub constitutes another significant requirement, which is especially crucial for use case 2 (truck-drone-tandem).
As described in Section 4.2, the drones must be able to take off from a relatively small area onboard the truck during a stop.
Later, after successfully delivering their parcels, they must return to the truck and land on it.
For efficiency reasons, the truck may have moved to a different stop location in the meantime.

The desired tolerance level for landing accuracy is ±5 cm for this use case, which we defined based on the dimensions of the logistic drone (EmQopter Drone) and the DHL city delivery truck in this study.
Diverse methodologies for landing on moving vehicles or ships have been explored and demonstrated with experimental outcomes within the scientific literature.

The majority of these strategies involves the utilization of optical sensors, such as RGB cameras, as evident in studies (Dhami et al., 2022, Gautam et al., 2022, Keipour et al., 2022, Meng et al., 2019, Mohammadi et al., 2020, Morales et al., 2023).
The extensive deployment of detection and tracking techniques serves as a cornerstone for planning the drone’s movement (Do Trong et al., 2021).
Rabelo et al. (2020) propose a solution for precise UAV landings on mobile platforms, like trucks.
It manages a cooperative formation between the mobile landing spot and UAV, allowing the UAV to land and take off from there.
Another study by Gupta et al. (2022) introduced and experimentally evaluated an approach enabling a group of heterogeneous drones to land on a moving platform.
They used an artificial potential field method to guide the drones, avoiding internal collisions and following visual tags.

One of the most popular commercially available systems for take-off and landing on a mobile platform is the Airbus DeckFinder Airbus (2023), which operates on the principle of an active sender and receiver.
This enables UAVs to autonomously take off and land with an accuracy of 10−20 cm in challenging missions under adverse environmental conditions, regardless of GNSS and impaired visibility conditions.
The existing literature primarily focuses on the autonomous landing and take-off of single UAVs on mobile platforms.

However, there is a notable research gap in addressing the challenges and solutions related to the simultaneous landing of multiple UAVs on the same mobile platform, which incorporates challenges related to collective detection, tracking, planning, and control.
As future research, further efforts need to be made to mitigate external disturbances, such as wind turbulence, through robust altitude control and precision landing planners.
In further studies, cooperative environmental perception, where the truck employs its own sensors and guides approaching drones with information from the ground, can also be investigated.
The challenges of safely executing landings in complex urban landscapes, coupled with the lack of comprehensive legal guidelines, highlight the need for future research.
Moreover, the legal frameworks governing landing maneuvers towards a mobile hub in a dynamic traffic environment deserve further investigation.
To enable safe autonomous drone operations, autonomous navigation is a basic requirement.
Navigation includes both flight path planning (Section 5.2.2) and self-localization.
The state-of-the-art for localization is based on several sensors and algorithms to determine an accurate position, altitude and attitude of the system.
Commonly used sensors include cameras, radio receivers, GNSS receivers, inertial measurement units (IMU) and distance sensors (lidar, radar).
All captured data is combined using sensor data fusion (Peng et al., 2020).
Stochastic state estimators, such as Kalman filters, are applied to determine the best possible state estimate based on the available noisy data.
Depending on the quality and availability of the sensor data, different levels of localization accuracy can be achieved.
Regarding the technical requirements for drones in the logistics sector, we distinguish between three different scenarios that require different levels of localization accuracy.
The first and least demanding scenario concerns flying in non-urban areas, where few to no obstacles and flying objects would be expected.
It is therefore assumed that a localization accuracy of 5 m is sufficient.
Nevertheless, the specifications of potential UTM systems, such as U-Space, should be complied with.
For the second scenario, flying in an urban environment, increased accuracy is required as the density of static and dynamic obstacles is significantly higher.
We assume that an accuracy of 1.5 m is necessary to ensure safe operation in urban areas.
The last and most demanding scenario includes all situations in which the drone has to take off or land in a certain predefined area, i.e. to unload or pick up a parcel or to recharge its battery.
Additionally, as this occurs primarily in the area of hubs where an increased volume of air traffic is expected, a particularly high level of positioning accuracy reduces the risk of collisions.
We therefore recommend a minimum accuracy of 0.3 m for this scenario.

Additionally, it should be mentioned that the flight maneuvers in these special situations should be supported by ground-based guidance sensors so that redundant and more precise localization accuracies are feasible, as required for example when landing on mobile platforms (Section 5.2.5).
For localization, current drone applications use a combination of the sensors and methods relying primarily on a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS).
The GNSS of the United States called Global Positioning System (GPS) and the European system called Galileo are well-known implementations.
A UAV that uses a GNSS for localization receives signals from several satellites and calculates its position based on the time of flight of each received satellite signal.
Self-localization stands as a significant attribute impacting risks in both aerial and ground domains.
The accessibility and precision of GNSS can present challenges within numerous operational settings.

For example, in urban environments, buildings can block or reflect direct line-of-sight between satellites and GNSS receivers, leading to navigational inaccuracies due to multipath effects or even total signal interruptions.
Moreover, atmospheric conditions can contribute to fluctuations in the accuracy of GNSS-based positioning (Bauranov and Rakas, 2021).
Within urban canyons, the positional error can escalate beyond 20 m due to signal obstructions (Causa et al., 2022, Niu et al., 2019).
As emphasized by Bijjahalli et al. (2019), the permissible error threshold should ideally remain below 3 m.
This underscores the necessity for improved positioning systems or alternative technologies to enhance outdoor localization accuracy.
However, not only limited signal reception caused by environmental conditions but also attacks on GNSS-based systems represent an increasing technical challenge.
A distinction is made between so-called spoofing and jamming attacks.
In spoofing attacks, the GNSS signal is faked or manipulated in order to provide the system with false position information.
As a result, the affected drone perceives an incorrect position and navigates incorrectly.
Spoofing attacks usually require specialized hardware and software to disrupt and manipulate the GNSS signal.
The study of Psiaki and Humphreys (2016) discusses various spoofing detection strategies to ensure safe drone operations.
A matrix is used to compare known attack and defense strategies and document the effectiveness of the methods.
It also emphasizes that there is a need for research and development to take better action against spoofing attacks.
During a jamming attack, the GNSS signal is overlaid or completely blocked by interference signals.
As a result, the GNSS receiver does not receive sufficient signals from the satellite.
Jamming attacks can occur either intentionally or unintentionally, for example via transmitters or electronic devices that unintentionally generate radio interference.
Encryption techniques or anti-jamming filters are used as countermeasures.
Kassas et al. (2022) also propose a SoOp-based method to avoid jamming attacks or generally unreliable GNSS signals.
There are several methods for self-localization of autonomous drones based on sensor data, even in unknown environments.
These can be employed to robustify GNSS-based localization methods (Sünderhauf et al., 2012).

Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) (Cadena et al., 2016), for example, is a widely used approach where the drone determines its position and creates a map of its environment at the same time.
Another approach, which is usually used in addition to the main localization system, is the signals of opportunity (SoOp) method (Kapoor et al., 2017).
Here, a software-defined radio (SDR) is used to receive signals from phone towers, WLAN routers, TV transmitters or satellite communication.
These signals are analyzed to extract information about signal strength, time of flight and other parameters.
Using this information, the drone can determine its position relative to the signal sources.
For the use case of drone-based delivery, where in many cases the operating environment is known a priori, it is feasible to predict a GNSS satellite constellation (Delamer et al., 2021).
This information enables the path planning algorithm to avoid these regions and thus ensure consistent and reliable GNSS localization.
Further methods of robustification involve procedures for the automated generation of machine-readable annotated 3D maps of the lower airspace.
This map material can provide an optional, extended geo-awareness service as part of the respective UTM.

Another option to address inaccuracies of the GNSS is a cooperative localization approach, where multiple receivers, including UAVs, simultaneously collect signals from satellites, sharing and processing data collectively to calculate highly accurate positions and timing information (Qu et al., 2023).
In the paper of Jiang et al. (2020), for example, GNSS-independent distance measurements between the drones are used for such a cooperative localization approach.
These methods enhance accuracy and resilience.
With regard to the localization of drones in the logistics sector, the following research priorities have been identified, some of which are already the subject of several scientific studies.

In order to protect drones and their cargo from spoofing and jamming attacks, reliable and comprehensive detection methods are required that enable to initiate countermeasures if an attack is detected.

Furthermore, robust methods such as SLAM and SoOp need to be further adapted and implemented into the drone system to ensure sufficiently accurate localization in the event of a GNSS failure or inaccuracy.
The generation and deployment of machine-readable annotated 3D maps of the lower airspace can also contribute to achieving this.

In general, algorithms and sensors are required that increase the localization accuracy in comparison to known methods, especially in order to meet the high requirements in hub areas or near parcel dropoff points.

Reliable and effective communication is essential, enabling the drone owner to command, control, coordinate, and monitor the activities of the drones as well as enabling the drone itself to transmit data to the UTM system.
Communication allows real-time updates for navigation, ensuring that drones adjust their waypoints during missions accordingly.
It also enables the transmission of valuable data collected by the drones, such as images, videos, and sensor readings for analysis and informed decision-making (Cao et al., 2018).
Furthermore, future UTM concepts (like the European U-Space) require the transmission of various data for identification and authorization reasons.

Additionally, permanent information about the drones mission and operation status such as position, altitude and planned flight path will be required, similar to the requirements for an airplane in ATM.
For these reasons, secure and reliable communication is essential.
In current UAV-applications so-called C2-links (Command and Control Link) are employed to establish robust communication between the ground station and the drone itself.
Depending on the distance between the ground station and the drone, different communication technologies can be employed or combined.
The related research on UAV communication is recently summarized in various papers (Deebak and Al-Turjman, 2020, Jin et al., 2023, Sharma et al., 2020).
For short ranges, radio frequencies such as UHF (ultra high frequency) or VHF (very high frequency) links can be utilized.
Since the drone-truck-tandem (use case 2) is operated mostly in urban airspace, where high efficiency and low latency are required, a direct communication link is considered to be suitable.
Based on the average flight distances identified in Section 4.3, a UAV with a minimum communication range of approximately 1 km can be employed.
Cellular networks such as 4G and 5G are another suitable option for drone communication, but may be unreliable in certain areas due to limited network coverage.

The utilization of drones within 5G wireless cellular communication networks has recently gained significant attention (Campion et al., 2018), as this technology facilitates higher bandwidths compared to previous communication methods.
Long-range scenarios in BVLOS operation, such as use case 1, usually require satellite-based communication in order to achieve a reliable C2-link.
Not only the GNSS and thus localization (Section 5.2.6), but also communication is at risk from targeted attacks.

Depending on the implementation of security measures and the ability of the attacker, it is possible to gain access to sensor data via the drone’s communication modules and transfer malicious information to the drone.
Cyber-attacks can cause irreparable damage to drones or allow the attacker to gain control.
The authors of Rani et al. (2016) demonstrate a commonly used hacking method on a commercial drone.
In addition, an overview of hacking attack and defense methods to overcome cyber-attacks on UAVs is given.

Due to the continuous development of new cyber-attack strategies, it is necessary to consider countermeasures such as encryption technologies, authentication procedures and firewalls for future investigations to prevent unauthorized access to drones in operation.
Another research gap comprises reliable and energy-efficient communication methods for short range and long-range applications, that also take into account UTM-specific requirements, such as U-Space.
The optimal recharging concept for a drone depends on the use-case at hand.
It is part of the general turn-around after each flight, which also includes cargo loading and system checks.

The flight itself should account for most of the overall mission time for economic reasons, therefore exchanging or charging the battery (or any other possible power source) needs to be of short duration.
A fully charged battery is favorable due to the fact that unforeseen incidents may occur during a mission, that would increase the duration of the flight.
These incidents involve maneuvers to avoid temporary obstacles or changing wind or weather conditions in general.
For optimizing mission profiles for individual UAVs and enhancing overall traffic management in specific airspace regions, battery consumption prediction is valuable.
Conte et al. (2022) introduce a deep learning-based approach for forecasting UAV battery consumption along a specified path, taking into account the effects of wind vectors.

Other studies like Pinto and Lagorio (2022) tackle the challenge of extending the operational range of drones from a network design perspective, providing them charging stations for recharging or automatic battery replacement, when their destination is beyond the battery capacity.
The necessary energy storage capacity is directly linked to the required transportation performance depending on the distance to be covered and the weight to be carried.
Sizing of the energy storage is especially critical for multi-copter UAVs in their respective use case.
For a first estimation with a payload of 2.5 kg, an energy-consumption of 22 Wh per kilometer can be assumed (Zhang et al., 2021).
Based on the size of the area of operation and the number (and locations) of available distribution points (delivery trucks), the range of possible flight distances can be obtained.
Combined with the aforementioned energy consumption, the battery system can then be specified.
Requirements for the operational framework of automated drone-based logistics.
Technical requirements for automated drone-based logistics.
Compared to long-range delivery in use case 1, the distances and flight times for last-mile deliveries in use case 2 are substantially shorter but are conducted at higher frequency.
Multi-copter drones do not fly as aerodynamically efficient as fixed-wing drones, which additionally demands to minimize unnecessary weight as much as possible.
As batteries constitute a substantial portion of the aircraft weight, their sizing must be carefully tailored to meet the specific mission requirements.
In last-mile delivery scenarios, the UAV returns to its starting point after each delivery to pick up new cargo and can therefore be refitted for the next task at hand.
Recharging a permanently installed battery is too time-consuming, so it needs to be replaceable in a quick and safe manner — ideally automated.

Having more drones on standby to compensate for those occupied with recharging is not feasible from an economic standpoint and would greatly impact the available space on the delivery truck, reducing its cargo volume.
The research gap is the need for further investigation in optimizing charging concepts, battery capacity, and energy management for drones in different use cases.
This includes exploring the implementation of automated charging stations, battery replacement systems on the ground and on the truck, and peer-to-peer networks to enhance flight time and efficiency.

Additionally, there is a need for research in battery consumption prediction, quick and safe battery replacement methods for multi-copter drones, and appropriately sizing energy storage capacity based on operational requirements.
In this paper, we investigated automated drone-based parcel delivery concepts.
Following a data-based demand analysis, the so-called **Hub(X)-to-X transport** and the **Truck-Drone-Tandem** were identified as technically and economically promising use cases.
The first one mentioned covers scenarios with different start and destination positions, e.g. from an arbitrary starting point to a hub or from a hub directly to a customer.
By using fixed wing VTOL drones, distances of up to 120 km can be covered.
Since long-distance drone delivery is independent of road conditions or traffic jams, it offers significant time-saving potential compared to conventional express or courier deliveries.
It is therefore particularly advantageous for time-critical applications, such as in the medical sector, or in regions with poor road conditions.

According to the conducted analysis, an average delivery hub in Germany would need to have approximately 91 long-distance drones available to meet the current demand for express and courier deliveries.
The truck-drone tandem is intended for last mile deliveries.
It holds efficiency potential especially in urban regions where many parcels have to be delivered in a relatively small area and a lot of traffic and few parking spaces are to be expected.

For this use case, two autonomous delivery drones operate together with a conventional delivery truck, which acts as a mobile micro hub and provides space for take-off and landing as well as automated parcel pick-up for the drones.

Based on our investigations the deployment of a truck-drone-tandem is capable to increase the performance to 240% in terms of delivered packages per time period compared to a conventional delivery truck.
Based on the average package volume, a demand of 129 truck-drone-tandems per hour was determined for a big city such as Munich.
The quantitative results of our investigation of use cases identified several technical challenges.

One central challenge, in order to enable scalable deployment of autonomous drones, is the technological capability to coordinate cooperating and non-cooperating drones in a shared airspace, such as a delivery hub.

Based on this, we conducted a comprehensive literature study and derived high-level technical requirements as well as research gaps that are essential to successfully implement drones in long-distance and last-mile delivery, taking into account an overall system perspective.

The results of these analyses with regard to the operational framework conditions and the technical requirements for drone-based logistics applications are summarized in Table A.5, Table B.6 in the Appendix.
They also contain identified research gaps, which were categorized as small (s), medium (m) or large (l).
